collection.title: Made by hand in Odisha
collection.lead: A cut piece of cloth. A brush held close. A silver thread bent into a pattern. Follow three crafts into the decisions—and the people—behind them.
collection.intro: Begin with an object that makes you stop. Stay for the question you want to ask its maker. This collection connects three traditions through photographs, sourced introductions and invitations to look more closely.

cards.title: Pipili · colour at the stitched edge
cards.text: Look at how separate shapes become a pattern, and how the maker’s tools bring them together.

cards.title: Pattachitra · read the painted line
cards.text: Begin with a small figure and let the border guide you towards its story.

cards.title: Cuttack · follow a silver thread
cards.text: Notice the spaces between the lines. Continue into the existing Tarakasi guide.

questions.heading: Notice
questions.text: Choose one edge, join or repeated motif. What makes you want a closer look?

questions.heading: Ask
questions.text: Who made this piece? Which stages did they work on? How did they learn?

questions.heading: Remember
questions.text: Ask for the maker’s preferred credit and permission before recording or sharing their story.

collection.limits: Three selected traditions, not a complete craft catalogue or an inspected workshop directory. The craft journey is a reading and planning collection; no day route, appointment, transfer or price has been verified.

paragraphs.text: In Rahul Mukherjee’s display photograph, circles repeat inside larger circles, with bright borders around them. The eye can follow one shape through the arrangement. That is a useful place to begin looking, before asking how the cloth was assembled.
D’source’s documented lampshade starts with coloured cloth cut and joined into appliqué. A cardboard stencil marks repeated outlines; the matching pieces are cut in layers and bundled for later use.

The appliqués are machine-stitched onto cloth in plain and decorative patterns. Wooden or iron rings then give the shade its shape. This is one documented process, not a description of every Pipili workshop.

Andrew Moore’s photograph brings the sewing machine into view beside the textile. It does not identify the maker or connect this piece to the lampshade example. Seeing a tool is a starting point for asking which stages it serves.
When speaking with a maker, ask about one edge or repeated shape. If you plan to buy, ask for the maker’s name, materials and care instructions, rather than trying to infer them from a photograph.

pages.title: Pattachitra: preparing a surface, learning a line

paragraphs.text: In the Government of Odisha’s account, cloth receives a coating of chalk and tamarind-seed glue before painting. Borders come first, then a brush sketch, flat colours and fine black outlines. Krishna and Jagannath are among the subjects. The smooth prepared surface and the successive marks are different parts of making the picture; this account does not establish the materials of every work today.

Joanna Williams describes large cloth paintings with narrative scenes around their edges. Her 1996 study also shows how painting was learned: pupils practised, filled images drawn by a teacher and worked on borders. A large picture could involve several hands. These are documented working relationships, not evidence that skill is inherited or that every painter belongs to the Chitrakara community.

To read a particular painting, ask the maker to identify its scene and the relationship between the central image and surrounding figures. Record the artist’s name and medium with the work. The photographs here show painting and display; they do not identify every figure, the materials used, or the unnamed makers’ community.
